questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess listing sample spaces; no probability calculation is requested.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–3 use Ω for the set of possible recorded outcomes and ordered tuples for successive results.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Includes ordered multistage outcomes, distinct sums and products, and simultaneous unordered selections.

classification.difficultyReason: Enumerate subsets including the empty and full events, using the supplied total of eight as a check, then assign probabilities from subset sizes.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 continues Section A above the new 25B band. Part (a) lists outcomes, part (b) enumerates subsets and part (c) applies the favourable-outcome formula.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines the sample space, defines events as subsets, demonstrates sample-space listing and gives probability as favourable outcomes divided by total equally likely outcomes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List subsets of a three-outcome sample space and calculate their probabilities by counting equally likely outcomes.

classification.difficultyReason: Enumerates all subsets of a four-outcome sample space and assigns their probabilities.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 continues 25A above the later 25B band. Its fair four-sided die directly assesses subset enumeration and favourable-outcome counting; theoretical-probability is the closest primary catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: List possible outcomes as the sample space; an event is any subset. For equally likely outcomes, divide the number of favourable outcomes by the total number of outcomes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Enumerates all subsets of a four-outcome sample space and assigns their probabilities.

classification.difficultyReason: Count favourable outcomes and divide by the total number of equally likely outcomes.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess theoretical probability by counting favourable outcomes. This question continues Section A above the new 25B band; the supplied topicId identifies 25B and requires coordinator reconciliation.
questions.methodNote: Use the sample space and Pr(E)=n(E)/n(Ω) for equally likely outcomes, as taught in 25A. Part (d) uses the ordinary six-sided die convention.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count favourable outcomes and divide by the total number of equally likely outcomes.

classification.difficultyReason: Count equally likely ordered outcomes from three successive draws without replacement.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses multistage probability by counting ordered outcomes; no complement, union or intersection is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 lists sample spaces for successive trials and calculates probability as favourable outcomes divided by equally likely outcomes. List all six ordered arrangements and count the single favourable arrangement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count equally likely ordered outcomes from three successive draws without replacement.

classification.difficultyReason: Count equally likely postings and subtract the arrangements with exactly one letter in each box.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 precedes the 25B topic band and its matching answer appears in Chapter 25 Section A. Counting postings and one-to-one assignments makes probability-perm-comb the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 gives probability as favourable outcomes divided by equally likely outcomes. Page 5 explains using the complementary event when it is easier to count.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count equally likely postings and subtract the arrangements with exactly one letter in each box.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct the unrestricted placement count and contrast it with successively decreasing choices for one letter per box before taking their ratio.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 precedes the 25B topic band and continues Section A. The counted-placement probability is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the ratio of favourable outcomes to all equally likely outcomes. Count placements by successive choices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Counts unrestricted placements and compares them with placements having exactly one letter in each box.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires identifying equally likely individual faces across all unit cubes and expressing their ratio algebraically.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 precedes the 25B topic band and matches Chapter 25 Section A question 8 in the original answers. Its directly assessed method is theoretical probability by counting faces.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines probability as the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires identifying equally likely individual faces across all unit cubes and expressing their ratio algebraically.

classification.difficultyReason: Reframe counting events as independent inclusion or exclusion decisions for each outcome, then generalise the count to n outcomes.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed concept is counting subsets representing events; set notation is the closest catalogue skill, supported by the multiplication principle.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines an event as any subset of the sample space. Question 9 extends this definition by counting two membership choices for each outcome.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalises events as subsets by counting the inclusion or exclusion of each outcome.

classification.difficultyReason: Count unordered pairs and identify edge-sharing pairs in a geometric arrangement.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 requires counting equally likely pairs of squares and the subset sharing an edge. This belongs to the continuation of 25A above the new 25B band.
questions.methodNote: Use the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of equally likely outcomes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count unordered pairs and identify edge-sharing pairs in a geometric arrangement.

classification.difficultyReason: Fix one edge, identify the remaining edges sharing either endpoint without counting crossings as vertices, and compare this count with all remaining edges.

questions.mappingNote: Question 11 precedes the 25B heading and belongs to Section A. Counting the possible second edges applies theoretical probability directly.
questions.methodNote: Use the ratio of favourable outcomes to all equally likely outcomes, as defined on page 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires counting edges incident to either endpoint while distinguishing vertices from unmarked crossings.

classification.difficultyReason: Count the vertices connected to a chosen vertex by each of three geometric relationships.

questions.mappingNote: Question 12 precedes the 25B topic band and belongs to Section A, confirmed by its answer appearing before the Section B heading. The directly assessed skill is theoretical probability.
questions.methodNote: Use the introductory formula: probability equals the number of favourable equally likely outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes. Fixing the first vertex leaves seven equally likely choices for the second vertex.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count the vertices connected to a chosen vertex by each of three geometric relationships.

classification.difficultyReason: Place elements into Venn regions, then interpret compound expressions by applying complements and unions or intersections in the correct order.

questions.mappingNote: Page 4 defines union and intersection; page 5 defines complement and Example 3 demonstrates the same Venn construction followed by set determination. These directly support every response in question 1.
questions.methodNote: Represent the sample space by a rectangle and events by overlapping circles. Intersection selects common elements, union selects elements in either event, and complement selects elements outside the event but within the sample space.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct a two-set Venn diagram and interpret twelve expressions involving complements, unions and intersections.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires counting intersections and complements of multiples, then combining disjoint events.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly combines the complement and addition rules for events defined by multiples of 2 and 3. The final part adds the two disjoint exclusive regions.
questions.methodNote: Count equally likely outcomes; interpret intersections and inclusive unions as taught on page 4, use complements from page 5, and use the addition law from page 7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires counting intersections and complements of multiples, then combining disjoint events.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate negative subject preferences into complementary and compound events, then apply the complement and addition rules.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b directly apply the complement rule. Part c applies the addition law followed by the complement rule. Part d identifies the inclusive union of the two negative preferences as the complement of enjoying both. The closest catalogue skill is probability-complement-addition.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 specifies inclusive or and defines union and intersection; page 5 teaches Pr(A') = 1 − Pr(A); pages 7–8 teach the addition law and substitution using decimal probabilities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate negative subject preferences into complementary and compound events, then apply the complement and addition rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses complements of dependent draws and excludes both monochromatic outcomes in part c.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b directly adapt Example 4. Part c subtracts the disjoint all-red and all-blue outcomes, combining the same without-replacement method with mutually exclusive addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses complements of dependent draws and excludes both monochromatic outcomes in part c.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses complements and decreasing probabilities for four draws without replacement; part c excludes two mutually exclusive outcomes.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b directly adapt Example 4 to four draws. Part c adds the mutually exclusive all-blue and all-red probabilities before taking the complement.
questions.methodNote: Page 6, Example 4 uses the complement of at least one red token and multiplies decreasing fractions for draws without replacement. Page 4 gives addition for mutually exclusive events.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses complements and decreasing probabilities for four draws without replacement; part c excludes two mutually exclusive outcomes.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses complementary events and three successive probabilities without replacement.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses complementary events and three successive probabilities without replacement.

classification.difficultyReason: Count excluded ordered dice outcomes and apply the complement rule, including square products and divisibility.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count excluded ordered dice outcomes and apply the complement rule, including square products and divisibility.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify and count the few complementary ordered outcomes for three dice.

questions.mappingNote: The complement rule is the main assessed method, supported by counting equally likely ordered dice outcomes.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 establishes the complement rule; page 6, Example 5, applies it to three-dice experiments. Count the outcomes giving sums of 17 or 18, then subtract their probability from 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify and count the few complementary ordered outcomes for three dice.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that an odd product requires all five dice to show odd numbers, then use the complement.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 directly extends the taught three-dice example to five dice, retaining its complement and independent-product method.
questions.methodNote: Example 5(b), printed page 245, calculates the probability of an even product by subtracting the probability that every die shows an odd number from 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that an odd product requires all five dice to show odd numbers, then use the complement.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the product is a multiple of 3 exactly when at least one die shows 3 or 6, then use the complementary event across four independent rolls.

questions.mappingNote: Question 10 applies the same method to divisibility by 3: the complement requires every die to avoid 3 and 6.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 uses the complement of a product property, multiplies independent single-die probabilities, and subtracts from 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that the product is a multiple of 3 exactly when at least one die shows 3 or 6, then use the complementary event across four independent rolls.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the complementary event and multiply the probabilities of four independent rolls.

questions.methodNote: Page 6, Example 5(a), calculates the probability of at least one six by subtracting the probability of no sixes from 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the complementary event and multiply the probabilities of four independent rolls.

classification.difficultyReason: Adapt the taught complement method to die rolls, express the threshold using repeated failure, and check neighbouring integer counts to establish the minimum.

questions.mappingNote: Question 12 applies the same method to a die: replace the coin's failure probability of 1/2 with 5/6 and retain the 90% threshold. No logarithmic shortcut is needed.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 on printed page 246 uses the complement of at least one success, raises the single-trial failure probability to n, and compares consecutive integer trial counts against the required threshold.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the complement across repeated independent rolls and compare consecutive integer trial counts with a probability threshold.

classification.difficultyReason: Uses the complement of all tails and compares consecutive trial counts to establish the minimum.

questions.mappingNote: Question 13 repeats Example 6's coin-toss minimum-trials task with a 95% threshold. The fair-coin convention follows that example.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 uses the complement of all tails, then compares consecutive powers of one half against the required failure probability.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses the complement of all tails and compares consecutive trial counts to establish the minimum.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines independent dice outcomes, a complementary event and four mutually exclusive positions for exactly one six.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a), (c) and (d) multiply probabilities for independent rolls; part (b) directly extends Example 5(a) to four rolls; part (e) adds four mutually exclusive single-six positions. The complement and addition rules are the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 6, Example 5(a), multiplies independent no-six probabilities and subtracts from 1 for at least one six. Page 4 explains addition of mutually exclusive event probabilities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines independent dice outcomes, a complementary event and four mutually exclusive positions for exactly one six.

classification.difficultyReason: For at least two whites, extend the complement method to exclude both zero and exactly one white, counting all five possible positions of the single white.

questions.methodNote: Page 5 defines the complement rule. Page 6, Example 5, finds an at-least-one probability by subtracting the probability of no successes, multiplying probabilities across independent trials.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Uses complementary events over five spins, including counting the five possible positions of exactly one white outcome.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify common and combined elements of two explicitly listed sets, count shared elements once, and divide each event count by ten.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify elements of two small sets, their intersection and their union, then count equally likely outcomes.

classification.difficultyReason: Add the probabilities of two mutually exclusive colours in a single draw.

questions.methodNote: Page 4 defines inclusive union and the addition rule for mutually exclusive events. Page 5 Example 2 applies that rule by adding favourable counts over a common total.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add the probabilities of two mutually exclusive colours in a single draw.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify intersections of familiar card categories and count favourable cards.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify intersections of familiar card categories and count favourable cards.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguishes intersections and inclusive unions of overlapping number properties.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguishes disjoint, overlapping and contained card events when applying inclusive or.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the addition law directly and rearrange it to find a missing event or intersection probability.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count multiples and subtract the overlap when two divisibility events are joined by inclusive or.
